findings.title: `fire_unit_until` cannot stop the minute unit early — `mt-run` blocks until the unit ends
findings.description:
The entire point of this diff (and of `fire_unit_until`) is to bound the cutover's minute firing to its trailing phase. The caller comment in `scripts/cutover_921_minute_sessions.py` says "the unit is stopped once that line lands and the timers own the backfill," and the test is literally named `test_the_minute_firing_stops_once_the_trailing_phase_completes`.

But `fire_unit_until` does this:
```python
run(["mt-run", *mt_run_args], sudo=True, check=False, stream=True)   # blocks
reached = wait_for_unit_or_line(unit, cursor, pattern)               # dead
if reached and unit_active(unit):
    ...stop_unit...
```
`run(...)` → `subprocess.run(...)` blocks until the child exits. The child is `sudo mt-run minute`, and `deploy/mt-run`'s `start_and_stream` runs `systemctl start --no-block` and then `while is_running "${unit}"; do sleep 2; done` — i.e., it does not return until the pass unit has fully ended. A minute pass is explicitly unbounded (trailing ~65k credits, then backfill to quota, ≈ the "ten hours" the docstring references), so `mt-run minute` blocks for that whole duration. By the time `wait_for_unit_or_line` runs, `unit_active` is already False, the stop branch never fires, and each cutover attempt still costs the full firing (up to `MAX_MINUTE_FIRINGS = 6`). The feature this diff adds does not do what it says.

The unit test hides this: `TestBoundedFiringAndRecord::_fire` patches `cutover_common.run` (so `mt-run` is a no-op that returns immediately), which is why the stop is observed in the test but not in production. Note `_fire_minute_pass` also discards the `reached` value (`cursor, _started, _reached`), so even the unreliable signal isn't consumed. This is exactly the "test passes on a shape the real data never uses" trap. To actually bound the firing, the cutover must not go through blocking `mt-run` for the start (e.g., `systemctl start --no-block` then poll), or the stop must happen while `mt-run` is still attached.

findings.title: `cagg_freshness_for_session` does not neutralize `last_successful_finish = '-infinity'`
findings.description:
The new probe reads `stats.last_successful_finish` raw:
```python
cur.execute("SELECT stats.last_successful_finish FROM timescaledb_information.jobs ... WHERE proc_name='policy_refresh_continuous_aggregate' AND job.hypertable_name=%s", (cagg,))
job_row = ...; last_refresh = job_row[0] if job_row else None
```
For a cagg refresh policy that has created but never successfully run, TimescaleDB reports `last_successful_finish = '-infinity'`. The codebase's own canonical helper explicitly guards this (`src/manta_trading/market/maintenance/cagg_freshness.py:78` uses `nullif(s.last_successful_finish, '-infinity'::timestamptz)`). This probe omits the guard, so on a freshly rebuilt / just-reinstalled 4h cagg (or a policy that has not yet succeeded), `CaggFreshness.stale` will compare against an unparseable/`-infinity` timestamp — a psycopg parse error or a permanent `WAIT` — rather than a clean "no refresh on record." It is unlikely on the running production host (the 4h policy refreshes hourly), but it is the one state where `--verify` should say "never refreshed, please wait" and instead misbehaves.

findings.title: `mt-minute-pass.timer` comment no longer matches the schedule
findings.description:
The first firing moved 01:05 → 04:05 UTC in this diff, but the justification comment above it was not updated:
```
# Staggered 30 minutes behind mt-daily-pass.timer so the two passes never
# start simultaneously ...
```
`mt-daily-pass.timer` fires at 00:35 and 12:35 UTC. 13:05 is indeed 30 min behind 12:35, but 04:05 is not 30 min behind 00:35. The "30 minutes behind" claim is now false for the first firing (the "never start simultaneously" property still holds). The sibling `mt-kalshi-pass.timer` comment was correctly updated in the same change to reference the new 04:05/13:05 pair, so the two timer files now disagree about why their schedules are staggered. Update the minute-timer comment to reflect the new rationale (fire after EODHD publishes the day).

findings.title: `manta-ops` grants the operator NOPASSWD `cat` of the full production env file
findings.description:
```
Cmnd_Alias MT_READ = /usr/bin/cat /etc/manta-trading.env
manta ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: MT_UNITS, MT_INSTALL, MT_READ, ...
```
`/etc/manta-trading.env` holds the production credentials (DB URL with password, EODHD key, Kalshi settings). The cutover's `verify_migrate_target` (`scripts/cutover_common.py`) only needs two keys from it — `MT_TIMESCALE_MAINTENANCE_URL` and `MT_TIMESCALE_DB_URL` — to confirm the maintenance URL targets the production database. A blanket `cat` of the whole file gives the operator account full credential read for the production database, which exceeds least-privilege: if the `manta` account is compromised, the attacker can read the prod DB password. The single-file grant is deliberate and narrow in scope, but consider restricting the readable set (e.g., a wrapper that echoes only the two required variables, or `grep` of specific keys) so the credential exposure matches the actual need.

findings.title: Per-chunk `fetch_session_bounds` query added on the acquire hot path
findings.description: Every chunk that carries a provider answer now opens a second pooled connection and runs `fetch_session_bounds` (a `trading_sessions` + `instruments` join) before judging the outcome. The trailing phase is one chunk/symbol (~13k extra small queries per cycle), and the unbounded backfill phase runs up to ~69 chunks/symbol, so this multiplies on the longest path. The query is window-bounded and cheap, and the session judgment is what makes the #22 fix correct, so this is acceptable — but it is a new per-chunk round-trip that was not present before. If backfill wall-clock regresses, batching the bounds per symbol (one query for the symbol's whole session range rather than per chunk) is the obvious follow-up.
